tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). content.text: 7,629 Dow closes saved. Now the day-by-day comparison: for each S&P trading day, compute the Dow's move over the exact same interval and flag days where the two disagree sharply.

input.command:
cd "/Users/avishjain/02-120 Project" && python3 - <<'EOF' 2>&1 | grep -v Warning
import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'.')
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from herding import market_data
spx = market_data.load_prices(market_data.MARKETS["spx_1928"])["Close"]
spx = spx[spx.index < "1953-01-01"]
dow = pd.read_csv("scratch/dow_check/dja_1927_1952.csv", parse_dates=["Date"], index_col="Date")["Close"]
both = spx.index.intersection(dow.index)
s, d = np.log(spx[both]), np.log(dow[both])
rs, rd = s.diff().dropna(), d.diff().dropna()
gap = rs - rd
print(f"{len(both):,} shared days, 1928-1952. S&P vs Dow daily moves: correlation {np.corrcoef(rs, rd)[0,1]:.3f}, "
      f"typical gap (sd) {gap.std():.2%}")
print("days where the S&P and Dow moves differ by more than 4 points:")
for day in gap[abs(gap) > 0.04].index:
    nxt = gap.index[gap.index.get_loc(day)+1] if gap.index.get_loc(day)+1 < len(gap) else None
    print(f"  {day.date()}  S&P {np.expm1(rs[day]):+6.1%}  Dow {np.expm1(rd[day]):+6.1%}   next day: S&P {np.expm1(rs[nxt]):+6.1%} Dow {np.expm1(rd[nxt]):+6.1%}")
EOF

def main(days=None, n=40):
    """All terms (or only those inside the last `days` days) against n model histories."""
    s = market_data.returns("spx_1928")
    s = s if days is None else s.iloc[-int(days):]
    x, mu, sd = s.values, s.values.mean(), s.values.std()
    with experiments.Pool() as pool:
        hs = experiments.histories(calibrate.load("spx"), calibrate.HELD_OUT_SEEDS[:n], len(x), pool=pool)
    runs = [(h["r"] - h["r"].mean()) / h["r"].std() * sd + mu for h in hs if h is not None]
    print(f"S&P 500 {s.index[0].year}-{s.index[-1].year}; {len(runs)} of {len(hs)} model histories did not run away")
    print("value (percentile among the model histories); falls are log returns\n")
    rows, sims_of = [], []
    for t in politics.terms(s.index):
        a, b = t["a"], t["b"]
        real, sims = measures(x[a:b], mu, sd), [measures(h[a:b], mu, sd) for h in runs]
        pct, fl = flags(real, sims)
        rows.append(dict(t, flags=fl, kinds=[kind(k, pct[k]) for k in fl]))
        sims_of.append(sims)
        cells = "  ".join(f"{k} {real[k]:.3g} ({pct[k]:.0f})" for k in KEYS if not np.isnan(real[k]))
        print(f"{t['name']:<10} {t['party']} {t['start'].year}-{t['end'].year} {b - a:>5,} days: {cells}"
              f"  -> {len(fl)} flags {', '.join(f'{k}:{w}' for k, w in zip(fl, rows[-1]['kinds']))}")
    # luck alone: each model history in turn plays the S&P against the others
    luck = np.array([[len(flags(sims[j], sims[:j] + sims[j + 1:])[1]) for sims in sims_of]
                     for j in range(len(runs))])
    total = sum(len(r["flags"]) for r in rows)
    print(f"\nluck alone: {luck.mean():.2f} flags per term; over {len(rows)} terms median "
          f"{np.median(luck.sum(1)):.0f}, 95th percentile {np.percentile(luck.sum(1), 95):.0f}. "
          f"S&P: {total} (reached by {np.mean(luck.sum(1) >= total):.0%} of luck runs)")
    counts, party = [len(r["flags"]) for r in rows], [r["party"] for r in rows]
    if len(set(party)) == 2:
        for P in "DR":
            c = [k for k, q in zip(counts, party) if q == P]
            print(f"{P}: {len(c)} terms, {sum(c)} flags = {np.mean(c):.2f} per term")
        diff, p = permutation_p(counts, party)
        print(f"D - R: {diff:+.2f} flags per term, permutation p = {p:.2f}")
    kinds = [w for r in rows for w in r["kinds"]]
    print(f"kinds of flag: wild {kinds.count('wild')}, calm {kinds.count('calm')}, "
          f"return {kinds.count('ret-high') + kinds.count('ret-low')}")
    for r, sims in zip(rows, sims_of):
        if r["name"] == "Roosevelt":           # how much the suspect 1930s closes matter
            i = s.index.get_indexer(pd.DatetimeIndex(SUSPECT))
            y = x.copy()
            y[np.concatenate([i, i + 1])] = 0.0
            print(f"Roosevelt without the {len(SUSPECT)} suspect days: flags "
                  f"{flags(measures(y[r['a']:r['b']], mu, sd), sims)[1]} (with them: {r['flags']})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
def test_spx_1928_great_crash_and_depression():
    r = data.returns("spx_1928")

def recessions(end=END):
    """NBER recession indicator by month (1 = recession) from FRED, up to END."""
    import ssl
    import certifi                       # trusted certificates (installed with yfinance)
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=certifi.where())
    with urllib.request.urlopen(FRED_URL, timeout=30, context=ctx) as resp:
        df = pd.read_csv(resp, parse_dates=["observation_date"])
    return df[df["observation_date"] <= pd.Timestamp(end)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- bad closes (November 2026)
# Yahoo's early S&P file has single wrong closes: a 6-10% "move" undone the next day while
# the Dow (MeasuringWorth) barely moved. Rule: S&P minus Dow beyond `gap` on a day AND beyond
# it the opposite way the next day, while the two days together agree within `agree`.

def _series(values, start="1935-01-02"):
    return pd.Series(values, index=pd.bdate_range(start, periods=len(values)), dtype=float)


def test_find_bad_closes_finds_a_planted_spike_and_nothing_else():
    ref = _series(100 * np.exp(np.cumsum(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.01, 300))))
    close = ref * 0.1 * np.exp(np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0, 0.002, 300))   # same market, small noise
    close.iloc[[50, 200]] *= [0.9, 1.08]                                         # two wrong closes
    assert list(data.find_bad_closes(close, ref)) == list(close.index[[50, 200]])


def test_find_bad_closes_keeps_a_real_crash_that_both_indexes_share():
    ref = _series([100, 101, 88, 89, 90])            # a real 13% fall that stays
    assert len(data.find_bad_closes(ref * 0.1, ref)) == 0


def test_listed_bad_closes_are_exactly_what_the_rule_finds_against_the_dow():
    spx = data.load_prices(data.MARKETS["spx_1928"])["Close"]
    dow = data.load_prices(data.DOW)["Close"]
    found = data.find_bad_closes(spx[spx.index <= dow.index[-1]], dow)
    assert [str(d.date()) for d in found] == list(data.BAD_CLOSES["spx_1928"])


def test_spx_1928_returns_skip_the_bad_closes():
    r = data.returns("spx_1928")
    s = data.load_prices(data.MARKETS["spx_1928"])["Close"]
    for d in data.BAD_CLOSES["spx_1928"]:
        assert pd.Timestamp(d) not in r.index
        # the next day's return now spans the two days, from the last good close
        i = s.index.get_loc(pd.Timestamp(d))
        assert r.loc[s.index[i + 1]] == pytest.approx(np.log(s.iloc[i + 1] / s.iloc[i - 1]))
    # after the fix, nothing left that the rule would flag
    dow = data.load_prices(data.DOW)["Close"]
    kept = s.drop(pd.DatetimeIndex(data.BAD_CLOSES["spx_1928"]))
    assert len(data.find_bad_closes(kept[kept.index <= dow.index[-1]], dow)) == 0

def fig8_out_of_sample(pool, p, path=FIG / "fig08_markets_model_never_saw.png", n=20):
    """Markets the calibration never saw: percentile of each among model histories."""
    keys = [k for k in stats.FINGERPRINT if k != "sd"]     # shape only: volatility differs by asset
    if not 1 <= n <= len(HELD_OUT) // 2:
        raise ValueError(f"n must be between 1 and {len(HELD_OUT) // 2}, got {n}")
    # (name, returns, seeds): the indexes use held-out seeds 1000-1019, the stocks
    # their own, 1020-1039, so the stocks are not compared with shorter copies of
    # the very histories the indexes were compared with.
    series = [("S&P 500 1928–", market_data.returns("spx_1928").values, HELD_OUT[:n]),
              ("Nasdaq-100 1985–", market_data.returns("ndx").values, HELD_OUT[:n])]
    series += [(t, market_data.stock_returns(t).values, HELD_OUT[n:2 * n])
               for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    cache, rows = {}, []
    for name, r, seeds in series:
        if (len(r), seeds) not in cache:
            cache[len(r), seeds] = [stats.fingerprint(x)
                                    for x in experiments.returns(p, seeds, len(r), pool=pool)]
        f = stats.fingerprint(r)
        rows.append([experiments.percentile(f[k], [s[k] for s in cache[len(r), seeds]]) for k in keys])
    rows = np.array(rows)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 9))
    cmap = matplotlib_diverging()
    im = ax.imshow(rows, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(rows.shape[0]):
        for j in range(rows.shape[1]):
            v = rows[i, j]
            ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                    color="white" if v < 10 or v > 90 else INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(keys)), [LABEL[k] for k in keys], rotation=30, ha="right")
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(series)), [s[0] for s in series], fontsize=8.5)
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.axhline(1.5, color="white", lw=3)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03)
    cb.set_label("percentile among model histories (50 = typical)")
    unusual = int(np.sum((rows < 5) | (rows > 95)))
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 0.95))
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 8. Markets the model never saw: two indexes and 20 stocks",
               f"Each cell: where a real market sits among {n} S&P-calibrated histories of the same length (0-100). "
               f"Middle colours = typical; dark ends = unusual (below 5 or above 95): {unusual} of {rows.size} cells. "
               "Volatility (sd) is left out: stocks move more than the index by nature. Stocks are price-only "
## Fig 8 — Markets the model never saw
[`fig08_markets_model_never_saw.png`](fig08_markets_model_never_saw.png). Percentile of each real market among 20 model
histories of the same length: the two indexes against seeds 1000–1019, the 20
stocks against their own seeds 1020–1039 (until November 2026 a length check was
off by one day and the stocks reused the index seeds; fixing it changed 49 unusual
cells to 43). **43 of 220 cells are unusual**: 6 of 20 for the indexes, 37 of 200 for
the stocks.
- **Stocks:** kurtosis is high (percentiles 70–100, median 95; 7 of 20 unusual), as
  expected: companies have their own jumps (earnings, lawsuits) on top of the
  market's. But their Hill tail exponent is typical (5–50, none unusual). The
  clearest miss is H of returns: 11 of 20 stocks sit at 100%, because the model's
  returns reverse from day to day and stocks' do not.
- **S&P since 1928:** unusual on memory (H and H|r| both 100%) and the paper-style α
  (0%), with clustering and 25-day kurtosis at the 95% edge: the 1930s were far
  wilder and longer-lasting than anything since.
- **Nasdaq-100 since 1985:** unusual on 3 of 10: 50-day clustering, H and 25-day
  kurtosis (all 100%).

## Fig 9 — How robust is it? (paper: "an open set of parameter values")

days. For seven measures we find the S&P's **percentile**, the share of histories below it
(50 = typical; 0 or 100 = none of the 40 did that). A measure outside 5–95 is a **flag**: the
model does not explain it.

**Luck check.** Letting each model history play the S&P against the other 39 gives 0.63 flags
per term, a median of 10 over 18 terms (95th percentile 19). The S&P gets **29**, reached by
only 2% of luck runs. So some misses are real.

**By party.** Democrats: 8 flags in 8 terms (1.00 per term). Republicans: 21 in 10 (2.10). If we
shuffle the party labels over the 18 terms, a gap this big turns up 24% of the time (36%
without the return measure), so it may well be luck. Hoover (5) and Bush 2001 (6) give 11 of
the 21 Republican flags; without them Republicans have 1.25 per term.

**By kind of event.** Three groups, each with both parties in it:
- *Long crises, too wild:* Hoover, Roosevelt, Bush 2001. Hoover had 36 crash days; no model
  history had more than 8 over the same days.
- *Calm eras, too quiet:* Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon (volatility percentile 0–2). All
  6 "too calm" flags fall in 1946–1980; only 1 of the 19 "too wild" flags does.
- *One shock day in a calm term:* 1946 (Truman), 1962 (Kennedy), 1987 (Reagan, a 20.5% fall in
  a day), 2025 (Trump): kurtosis at the 95th–100th percentile.

**What it means.** The misses follow the era and the kind of event, not the party. Herding
makes calm and wild spells, but they don't last long enough: the real market stayed wild for
years and calm for a decade. And real shocks can strike a calm market out of the blue, like
outside news; the model's news is a mild bell curve, so its big days come from herding.

**Limitations.** Only 40 histories, so percentiles move in steps of 2.5. The model's returns
reverse a little from day to day (H 0.39, Fig 7), so its multi-year returns spread too little
and return flags come too easily. Terms run from 291 to 3,023 days; long terms show misses more
easily. The Yahoo data probably has bad closes: 1935-04-16 (−10.5%, undone the next day) and
four similar 1935–1938 days, unchecked against another source. Removing all five takes away
Roosevelt's volatility flag; its kurtosis and crash-day flags stay.

are **single shock days in calm markets** (1946, 1962, 1987, 2025). So herding makes wild and
calm spells, but they don't last as long as real ones, and a sudden outside shock is not

content.text:
I got the suspect days verified: they were wrong closes in the Yahoo data, and I found 6 more of the same kind. All 11 are now left out when the data loads, and the affected figures and docs are updated.

**How I verified it**
- **Second source:** I got the Dow Jones average's daily closes for 1927–1952 from MeasuringWorth, a standard source for historical price data. The S&P and the Dow move almost together; on a normal day their moves differ by only about 0.55 points.
- **The five suspects:** on each of those days the Dow barely moved while your S&P file showed a 6–10% swing that reversed the next day. For example, on 16 Apr 1935 the S&P file shows −10.0%, while the Dow closed *up* 0.4%.
- **S&P's own record agrees:** the S&P 500's published list of its largest daily moves doesn't include any of these days, though a fall that size would have to be on it.
- **Six more found:** checking all 6,244 days found 6 more bad closes with the same pattern. They are 31 Mar 1930, 7 Jan 1931, 17 May 1934, 16 Dec 1935, 6 Jan 1938 and 3 Sep 1946. On 3 Sep 1946 the crash was real (the Dow fell 5.6%), but the S&P close was about 4% too low.
- **Real crashes stay:** the 1929 crash and 18 Oct 1937 are confirmed by both indexes, and the rule keeps them.

**What I changed**
- `herding/market_data.py`: a new tested function, `find_bad_closes`, and a list of the 11 dates, `BAD_CLOSES`. Loading the 1928 data now skips those closes, so the next day's return runs from the last good close and no price is made up.
- `data/dow_jones_daily_1927_1952.csv`, plus a download step in `data/download_market_data.py`, so the check can be repeated.
- `scripts/analysis/president_terms.py`: the old "without the 5 suspect days" workaround is removed.
- 4 new tests: a planted spike gets caught, a real crash doesn't, the rule finds exactly the 11 listed dates, and nothing is left to flag afterwards.

**What changed in the results**
- **Fig 8:** essentially no change, still 43 of 220 unusual cells.
- **Fig 12:** the Democrat–Republican return gap is still +6.8% a year. It now beats 97% of the shifted calendars instead of 98%. Volatility, tails and crashes still show no party difference.
- **Fig 12b:**
  - Truman loses his only flag: his 1946 "shock day" was a bad close (kurtosis 12.9 → 7.0).
  - Roosevelt's flags go from 3 to 4.
  - Democrats now have 10 flags in 8 terms (was 8). The party gap could come from chance **37%** of the time (was 24%), so "the misses follow the era, not the party" is now *stronger*.
  - Clinton's and Obama's returns crossed the 95% line, adding a flag each. RESULTS.md now notes how close to that line these flags sit.

I updated RESULTS.md (Fig 12 table, Fig 12b text and the whole term table), KEY_POINTS.md, GALLERY.md, and the data list in CLAUDE.md. I rebuilt the term table from the script's own functions rather than copying numbers by hand. All **562 tests pass**.

Nothing is committed yet. These changes and the email-hiding fix can go in one commit, with a message from you.

# Can Herding Explain Market Crashes?

## Who I am
I'm Avish, an undergraduate in 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026).
This repository is my final project. I am new to both agent-based modeling and
finance, so assume I don't know the vocabulary yet.

## How I like to learn
- Teach me one idea at a time, in plain language, and define each term before you use it.
- Quiz me with small exercises instead of asking "does that make sense?" (use the
  `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill when I'm learning the science or the paper).
- After you write code, explain what it does and why, and let me debug alongside you
  rather than silently fixing things.
- Prove that code is right, not just that it runs (use the `test-every-function` skill).

## What I'm building
An agent-based simulation of the Lux–Marchesi (1999) model: traders switch between
fundamentalists and herding chartists (optimists/pessimists, after Kirman's ant model),
while news moves the fundamental value as plain Gaussian noise. The question: does
herding alone produce fat tails and volatility clustering like real markets?
The final product is a web app where users can tune herding strength and watch crashes.

### Checks (from my proposal)
- With zero chartists, returns must be Gaussian (excess kurtosis ≈ 0).
- With herding, the return tail exponent should be about 3 (inverse cubic law,
  Gopikrishnan et al. 1998), and S&P 500 data should show this too.
- Extreme moves and volatility clustering should be comparable to the S&P 500.
- Later: reproduce Kirman's ant model first as a check against his math.

## Where things live
Top level: `herding/` (code), `scripts/` (things to run), `figures/` (things to look at), `docs/` (things to read),
`data/`, `settings/`, `tests/`, `journal/`, `scratch/`. Run scripts from the project folder, e.g. `python3 scripts/main.py`.
- `docs/KEY_POINTS.md`: self-contained guide to the project for someone new to it (ideas, figures, findings, limits)
- `docs/SPEC.md`: the model's equations, each with its source (rebuild of November 2026). Code and spec must agree.
- `scripts/main.py`: quick comparison (S&P 500 vs 20 held-out S&P-calibrated histories), saves `figures/fig00_quick_check_sp500_vs_model.png`
- `scripts/make_figures.py`: makes `figures/fig01-fig12*.png` (descriptive names), explained in `figures/RESULTS.md`; `figures/GALLERY.md` shows them all with plain captions
- `herding/`: the program, one module per job
  - `model.py`: the Lux-Marchesi simulation from SPEC.md (numba-accelerated), runaway guard
  - `stats.py`: tail exponents (Hill and the paper's regression), kurtosis, autocorrelation, DFA/Hurst H,
    multi-day returns, and the `fingerprint` of a market
  - `market_data.py`: loads and checks the files in `data/`
  - `kirman.py`: Kirman's ant model with its exact solution (the herding check from the proposal)
  - `calibrate.py`: two fits (`python3 -m herding.calibrate paper|spx [--draws N] [--refine]`), each ending
    with a stability screen (100k-day runs on seeds 2000-2019) -> `settings/paper_matched.json`
    (reproduces the paper's numbers) and `settings/sp500_calibrated.json` (reproduces the S&P 500)
  - `experiments.py`: many histories in parallel, percentiles, the typical history
  - `policy.py`: extension: circuit breakers and a policy surprise (paired runs), used by Fig 11
  - `politics.py`: extension: the president's party (1923-2026) and its return gap against luck, used by Fig 12
  - `plots.py`: palette and drawing helpers (reusable by the future web app)
- `.vscode/`: VS Code setup (hides clutter, one-click tasks for tests and figures, suggested extensions)
- `settings/`: the two fitted settings
- `tests/`: one test file per module; `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` (quick: add `-m "not slow"`)
- `scripts/analysis/`: scripts behind individual findings (see its README; older versions are in git history)
- `docs/proposal.pdf`: my project proposal; `docs/course_project_guide.pdf`: the course's project handout
- `data/`: made by `data/download_market_data.py` (all series end 2026-10-30): S&P 500 1950- and 1928- (Yahoo ^GSPC),
  Nasdaq-100 (^NDX, 1985-), `stocks/` (20 large stocks with market beta 0.9-1.1, 2000-), VIX, NBER recessions (FRED USREC),
  Dow Jones 1927-1952 (MeasuringWorth; used to find 11 wrong closes in the 1928 S&P file)
- `docs/papers/`: sources. The Lux & Marchesi Nature paper (doi:10.1038/17290) is `docs/papers/LuxMarchesi1999_Nature.pdf`,
  kept locally only (git-ignored: copyrighted, and this repo is public). The equations come from the
  Samanidou et al. (2007) review (see SPEC.md); the parameter tables of Lux & Marchesi (2000) are still
  needed via CMU library access.
- `docs/`: everything to read (KEY_POINTS, SPEC, proposal, papers/), plus my notes from tutoring sessions; `docs/journal_guide.md` points to the key moments in `journal/`
- `scratch/`: temporary files (git-ignored)
- `journal/`: build journal logs (copied automatically; don't edit by hand)

## Working rules
- Keep the smallest working version checked before adding features.
- Commit messages should be in my own words; ask me for one if I haven't given it.
- This repo is public: never put passwords, API keys, or personal info in it.

# Can Herding Explain Market Crashes?

## Who I am
I'm Avish, an undergraduate in 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026).
This repository is my final project. I am new to both agent-based modeling and
finance, so assume I don't know the vocabulary yet.

## How I like to learn
- Teach me one idea at a time, in plain language, and define each term before you use it.
- Quiz me with small exercises instead of asking "does that make sense?" (use the
  `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill when I'm learning the science or the paper).
- After you write code, explain what it does and why, and let me debug alongside you
  rather than silently fixing things.
- Prove that code is right, not just that it runs (use the `test-every-function` skill).

## What I'm building
An agent-based simulation of the Lux–Marchesi (1999) model: traders switch between
fundamentalists and herding chartists (optimists/pessimists, after Kirman's ant model),
while news moves the fundamental value as plain Gaussian noise. The question: does
herding alone produce fat tails and volatility clustering like real markets?
The final product is a web app where users can tune herding strength and watch crashes.

### Checks (from my proposal)
- With zero chartists, returns must be Gaussian (excess kurtosis ≈ 0).
- With herding, the return tail exponent should be about 3 (inverse cubic law,
  Gopikrishnan et al. 1998), and S&P 500 data should show this too.
- Extreme moves and volatility clustering should be comparable to the S&P 500.
- Later: reproduce Kirman's ant model first as a check against his math.

## Where things live
Top level: `herding/` (code), `scripts/` (things to run), `figures/` (things to look at), `docs/` (things to read),
`data/`, `settings/`, `tests/`, `journal/`, `scratch/`. Run scripts from the project folder, e.g. `python3 scripts/main.py`.
- `docs/KEY_POINTS.md`: self-contained guide to the project for someone new to it (ideas, figures, findings, limits)
- `docs/SPEC.md`: the model's equations, each with its source (rebuild of November 2026). Code and spec must agree.
- `scripts/main.py`: quick comparison (S&P 500 vs 20 held-out S&P-calibrated histories), saves `figures/fig00_quick_check_sp500_vs_model.png`
- `scripts/make_figures.py`: makes `figures/fig01-fig12*.png` (descriptive names), explained in `figures/RESULTS.md`; `figures/GALLERY.md` shows them all with plain captions
- `herding/`: the program, one module per job
  - `model.py`: the Lux-Marchesi simulation from SPEC.md (numba-accelerated), runaway guard
  - `stats.py`: tail exponents (Hill and the paper's regression), kurtosis, autocorrelation, DFA/Hurst H,
    multi-day returns, and the `fingerprint` of a market
  - `market_data.py`: loads and checks the files in `data/`
  - `kirman.py`: Kirman's ant model with its exact solution (the herding check from the proposal)
  - `calibrate.py`: two fits (`python3 -m herding.calibrate paper|spx [--draws N] [--refine]`), each ending
    with a stability screen (100k-day runs on seeds 2000-2019) -> `settings/paper_matched.json`
    (reproduces the paper's numbers) and `settings/sp500_calibrated.json` (reproduces the S&P 500)
  - `experiments.py`: many histories in parallel, percentiles, the typical history
  - `policy.py`: extension: circuit breakers and a policy surprise (paired runs), used by Fig 11
  - `politics.py`: extension: the president's party (1923-2026) and its return gap against luck, used by Fig 12
  - `plots.py`: palette and drawing helpers (reusable by the future web app)
- `.vscode/`: VS Code setup (hides clutter, one-click tasks for tests and figures, suggested extensions)
- `settings/`: the two fitted settings
- `tests/`: one test file per module; `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` (quick: add `-m "not slow"`)

  Nasdaq-100 (^NDX, 1985-), `stocks/` (20 large stocks with market beta 0.9-1.1, 2000-), VIX, NBER recessions (FRED USREC),
  Dow Jones 1927-1952 (MeasuringWorth; used to find 11 wrong closes in the 1928 S&P file)
- `docs/papers/`: sources. The Lux & Marchesi Nature paper (doi:10.1038/17290) is `docs/papers/LuxMarchesi1999_Nature.pdf`,

- `docs/`: everything to read (KEY_POINTS, SPEC, proposal, papers/), plus my notes from tutoring sessions; `docs/journal_guide.md` points to the key moments in `journal/`
